catalog_status_note: Cancelled for lack of snow (Michigan Snowboard Museum timeline).

name: 1984 National Snurfing Championships
description: Museum timeline says the national snurfing championships ended after this period as snowboard technology outran the Snurfer; no edition is recorded for 1985.

name: 20th Annual Neil Edgeworth Memorial Banked Slalom
description: Record field of 320 riders aged 6 to 63, on the natural gully beside the Ridge Rocket chair. $5,000 split among the pro winners plus $10,000 across the other categories. Stephanie Haines became the first rider to win the female pro category four years running.

name: 22nd Neil Edgeworth Memorial Banked Slalom
description: BC Snowboard's 2019 results index links a finals results PDF for the 22nd NEBS. Podiums not yet harvested.

name: 25th Neil Edgeworth Memorial Banked Slalom
description: 25th anniversary edition, organised with BC Snowboard. Dates not given in the source (article posted 1 April 2024).
venue_name: TELUS Park, Big White Ski Resort

name: 26th Neil Edgeworth Memorial Banked Slalom
description: 255 riders entered, from juniors to riders in their sixties. Big White reported Chris Bradley as the fastest men's time (given as 1:26:51 in the source).

name: 27th Annual Neil Edgeworth Memorial Banked Slalom
description: Two runs, one Saturday and one Sunday, on either the Traditional Gully or the TELUS Park course. Pro (female/male open), amateur (ten age groups from 11-and-under to 60+, plus Pro Masters 40+) and para (female/male open) divisions.

name: Nescafe Open Champs 2010
description: Swatch TTR 4-Star halfpipe. The contest returned to Leysin after three seasons in Valais, with Nescafe back as title sponsor after previously backing it from 1994 to 2006. Return to Leysin after three seasons in Valais, and the return of Nescafé as title sponsor (a partner from 1994 to 2006). Announced as a Swatch TTR 4Star halfpipe competition. Exact dates not stated in the article I opened.

name: 20th NESCAFE Champs
description: 20th anniversary edition. Swatch TTR 4-Star, USD 50,000 prize purse and 850 TTR world ranking points to the winners. Slopestyle course combined kickers, a halfpipe and a wallride; warm spring-like conditions across the region but the course held up. The World Snowboard Guide report is dated 12 February 2011; exact competition dates were not given. Billed as the 20th anniversary of the Nescafé Champs Leysin and as the oldest snowboard event in Europe. Slopestyle course combining kickers, a halfpipe and a wallride. Winners took USD 50,000 and 850 Swatch TTR world ranking points, which corresponds to a 5Star rating.

name: 21st Nescafé Champs
description: 21st edition. Not present in the wave-1 edition list.

name: Nescafe Champs 2013
description: TTR 5-Star. Course again ran a halfpipe into the classic slopestyle kickers and rails.

name: 2008 Nissan X-Trail Nippon Open
description: 5Star event on the TTR tour, reported as drawing over 40,000 spectators. The parkstyle finals ran after heavy snow and high winds earlier in the week, with semi-finals and finals held back to back; Mikkel Bang and Jenny Jones won. Winners took 8,000 points toward the Burton Global Open Series championship.

name: 2009 Nissan X-Trail Nippon Open
description: Fifth stop of the 2008/09 Burton Global Open Series, as announced in the series calendar.

name: NISEKO MOIWA BANKED SLALOM 2025
description: Five divisions: snowskate, ski, snowboard elementary, snowboard open (junior-high and up) and snowboard master (43+). Entries opened 15 March. Official site moiwabankedslalom.com.
catalog_status_note: Scheduled for 29 March with 30 March held as a bad-weather reserve day; practice on 28 March.

name: 2026 BANKED SLALOM TGK supported by Gyunyu Sekken (Tsugaike round)
description: Second race of the three-round North Alps Banked Slalom series (Hakuba Iwatake, Tsugaike, Hakuba Happo-one). Expanded to two days with 260 participants a day; ski, snowboard, snowbike and parent-child divisions added to the previously snowboard-only programme. Top six in each category awarded. Main sponsor Milk Soap (Gyunyu Sekken), supported by Red Bull Japan among others.
venue_name: Tsugaike Mountain Resort, Hannoki Special Course

name: 1987 North American Championships
description: Covered in the debut issue of TransWorld SNOWboarding (fall 1987) as the 'North American Championships in Banff, Canada'. No venue, dates, format or podium given.

name: Norwegian Snowboard Championships 2011
description: Halfpipe at Oslo Vinterpark on 27 March 2011; boardercross, big air and slopestyle at Trysil. Rated 3-Star TTR. Fields spanned ages 12 to 37. Silje Norendal, then 17, took two golds, two silvers and the King's Cup.

name: 7th Oakley Girlsessions
description: Swatch TTR 3-Star. Programme combined the TTR slopestyle with a team contest, a pipe competition and a freeski slopestyle, and was open to riders of all ability levels.

name: 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics
description: First Olympic snowboarding. Four medal events, men's and women's giant slalom and halfpipe. Held under FIS jurisdiction rather than the snowboarders' own ISF, which prompted a boycott of qualification by Terje Haakonsen. Dates are the first and last day of snowboarding competition as listed by Olympedia, not the dates of the Games as a whole.
venue_name: Mt. Yakebitai, Shiga Kogen (giant slalom) / Kanbayashi Sports Park (halfpipe)

name: 2002 Salt Lake City Winter Olympics
description: Giant slalom was replaced by parallel giant slalom. Olympedia records 118 athletes from 19 nations. Dates are the first and last day of snowboarding competition as listed by Olympedia, not the dates of the Games as a whole.

name: 2006 Torino Winter Olympics
description: Snowboard cross (boardercross) added for men and women, taking the programme to six medal events. Dates are the first and last day of snowboarding competition as listed by Olympedia, not the dates of the Games as a whole.

name: 2010 Vancouver Winter Olympics
description: Six medal events, athletes from 27 nations per Olympedia. Dates are the first and last day of snowboarding competition as listed by Olympedia, not the dates of the Games as a whole.

name: 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics
description: Slopestyle and parallel slalom both made their Olympic debut; 10 medal events, 237 competitors from 31 nations per Olympedia. Parallel slalom has not been held at any subsequent Games. Dates are the first and last day of snowboarding competition as listed by Olympedia, not the dates of the Games as a whole.

name: 2018 PyeongChang Winter Olympics
description: Big air made its Olympic debut and parallel slalom was dropped. 10 medal events, 244 competitors from 29 nations per Olympedia. Dates are the first and last day of snowboarding competition as listed by Olympedia, not the dates of the Games as a whole.

name: 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics
description: Mixed team snowboard cross added, taking the programme to 11 medal events. Big air was held at Big Air Shougang, a permanent ramp on a former steelworks site in Beijing; all other events at Genting Snow Park. Dates are the first and last day of snowboarding competition as listed by Olympedia, not the dates of the Games as a whole.
venue_name: Genting Snow Park, Zhangjiakou / Big Air Shougang, Beijing

name: 2026 Milano-Cortina Winter Olympics
description: Most recent Games as of September 2026. 11 medal events, 234 competitors from 27 nations per Olympedia. Dates are the first and last day of snowboarding competition as listed by Olympedia, not the dates of the Games as a whole.
venue_name: Mottolino Montagna del Divertimento / Carosello 3000, Livigno

name: O'Neill Evolution 2006
description: Launch year. Inferred from World Snowboard Guide's statement that the event ran for eight years from its 2006 launch and had no 2014 edition; no per-year source opened for this edition.

name: O'Neill Evolution 2007
description: Inferred from World Snowboard Guide's 'eight years since its 2006 launch'; no per-year source opened.

name: O'Neill Evolution 2008
description: Inferred from World Snowboard Guide's 'eight years since its 2006 launch'; no per-year source opened.

name: O'Neill Evolution 2009
description: Inferred from World Snowboard Guide's 'eight years since its 2006 launch'; no per-year source opened. A worldsnowboarding.org event page for O'Neill Evolution 2009 exists in search indexes but now returns 404.

name: O'Neill Evolution 2010
description: Halfpipe run as a TTR 6Star, slopestyle as a 5Star.

name: O'Neill Evolution 2011
description: Four contests in the week: halfpipe and slopestyle, both 6Star, both for men and women. First year women started in both disciplines alongside the men.

name: O'Neill Evolution 2012
description: Referenced by Whitelines alongside the 2013 edition; exact dates not found in a source I opened.

name: O'Neill Evolution 2013
description: Big air run as a 6Star and halfpipe as a 5Star; 120 competitors, USD 150,000 in prize money, entry limited to the TTR top 100. Last edition of the series.

name: O'Neill Evolution 2014
description: Recorded as a not-held year rather than an edition.
catalog_status_note: No event held. O'Neill marketing director Claudio Curiger said the brand was working on a new strategy and that major events were 'no longer an issue for the time being'. O'Neill kept other Davos commitments such as park sponsorship and its flagship store.

name: 1989 OP Pro of Snowboarding
description: Single-source (Snowboarder/TransWorld 1980s timeline: 'OP Pro of Snowboarding held at June Mountain, California'). No dates, no podium. Disciplines inferred from Craig Kelly's published career timeline, which lists halfpipe and giant slalom results at a 1989 OP Pro - a rider biography, so not used for placings.

name: 1991 OP Wintersurf
description: February 1991. Won by professional surfer Gary Elkerton, which the magazine used to make the point that surfing is harder to pick up than snowboarding. Single source.

name: 1st PacWest Banked Slalom
description: Inaugural edition, created and organised by Marcel Dolak with Karter Riach, Olivia Cayley and volunteer diggers. Exact dates not given in the sources found.
venue_name: Summit East, The Summit at Snoqualmie

name: 2024 PacWest Banked Slalom
description: 290 riders in attendance. Exact dates not given in the source.
venue_name: Summit East, The Summit at Snoqualmie

name: 5th Annual PacWest Banked Slalom
description: Scheduled for March 13-15, 2026 as the fifth annual event, with 21 divisions for ages 6 to 60+.
catalog_status_note: Cancelled for insufficient snow.
venue_name: Summit East, The Summit at Snoqualmie

name: Horsefeathers Pleasure Jam 2009
description: Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour 4-Star, USD 15,000 prize purse. Separate judging for female riders and an open-public-park category for less experienced entrants.

name: Pleasure Jam Vol. 13
description: First tour stop of the World Snowboard Tour northern-hemisphere season and of the QParks Snowboard Tour; contested on a pro kicker line.
catalog_status_note: Originally scheduled for early November 2015 and postponed: the Superpark opened on 24 October but snow was insufficient to build a compliant World Snowboard Tour International setup.

name: Pleasure Jam 2016
description: Opening stop of the 2016/17 QParks Snowboard Tour.

name: QParks Snowboard Tour 2016/17
description: Seventh season, EUR 40,000 total prize money. Ten stops: Pleasure Jam, Superpark Dachstein (19 Nov 2016); Battle ROJal, Snowpark Schoeneben (7 Jan 2017); Penken Battle, Vans Penken Park (14 Jan); Blue Tomato Plan P, Superpark Planai (28 Jan); Nock'n'Rock, Snowpark Turracher Hoehe (11 Feb); Sick Trick Tour Open, Snowpark Kitzbuehel (18 Feb); Gold & Glory Golden, Roofpark Axamer Lizum (25 Feb); Oakley Schilthorn Open, Skyline Snowpark Schilthorn (11 Mar); Shred Masters Feldberg, Badenova Snowpark Feldberg (18 Mar); Roof Battle, Superpark Dachstein (22 Apr). Covers Austria, Germany, Italy and Switzerland.

name: 3rd Annual Rattlesnake Banked Slalom
description: Six divisions, each capped at 25 riders; fastest of two runs, second run as tiebreaker.

name: VIII Rey del Park
description: Eighth edition and the first to count for the WSF South America Tour. WSF/TTR 2-Star slopestyle, USD 3,000 prize money, around 80 professional athletes from Chile, Argentina, Brazil, Spain, the USA and Canada.
city: Farellones / Lo Barnechea, Santiago Metropolitan Region

name: Lippi Rey del Park 2013
description: USD 8,000 in prizes; open to skiers as well as snowboarders. Described by the WSF as taking place in the best terrain park in South America.
city: Farellones / Lo Barnechea, Santiago Metropolitan Region

name: Roxy Chicken Jam Europe 2006
description: Wikipedia gives Kaprun; the WSF's provisional 06/07 women's tour calendar, published 24 October 2006, listed the European Roxy Chicken Jam at St Moritz, Switzerland. The two sources disagree on venue.

name: Roxy Chicken Jam US 2007 (finals)
description: The season-defining event of the 2006/07 TTR women's tour, where the women's TTR world champion was decided.

name: Roxy Chicken Jam Europe 2007
description: Second Roxy Chicken Jam of the 2007 calendar year; opens the 2007/08 women's season.

name: Roxy Chicken Jam US 2008
description: Wikipedia records a projected purse of over USD 150,000 for the 2008 US event, one of the largest in women's snowboarding at the time. Exact dates not given.

name: 2002 Empire Shakedown (first edition)
description: Inaugural edition, founded by Brendan O'Dowd and Patryck Bernier. Reported 6,000 spectators and a $10,000 winner-take-all purse.

name: 2003 Empire Shakedown
description: SnowboardQuebec's provincial history records Guillaume Brochu as the 2003 winner (not recorded as a result row in this wave).

name: 2005 Empire Shakedown
description: SnowboardQuebec records Matt Dano as the 2005 winner (not recorded as a result row in this wave).

name: 2006 Empire Shakedown
description: Sebastien Toutant, aged 13, was moved up from the amateur division and won the pro category in his first major contest.

name: 2008 Empire Shakedown
description: SnowboardQuebec records Charles Reid as the 2008 winner (not recorded as a result row in this wave). Last edition under Empire title sponsorship.

name: 2009 Ride Shakedown
description: First year with Ride Snowboards as title sponsor. SnowboardQuebec records Sebastien Toutant winning for a second time, aged 16 (not recorded as a result row in this wave).

name: 2010 Ride Shakedown
description: First year the series ran a US stop as well, at Snoqualmie, Washington on 12-13 March 2010.

name: 2011 Ride Shakedown
description: Series ran stops in Germany, the USA and Canada this year; Canadian dates not given in the source. SnowboardQuebec records Sebastien Toutant winning a third time.

name: 2015 Shakedown
description: Last edition listed by the event's own edition table. SnowboardQuebec's timeline places a cancelled Shakedown season in its 2015 entry, and CBC reported a Shakedown cancellation in January 2016 for lack of sponsorship and snow; whether the 2015 contest ran and the 2016 one was cancelled is unresolved - see open questions.

name: 1997 Showcase Showdown (first edition)
description: Whistler Blackcomb's 60th anniversary timeline dates the first Showcase Showdown to 1 February 1997. Snowboard Magazine's billing of the 2015 event as the 18th annual implies a 1998 start instead; the discrepancy is unresolved. The Whistler Museum separately records a Showcase Snowboards halfpipe competition on Blackcomb in 1992, won in the male 18-plus category by Whistler's Robin Dow, which may be a predecessor.

name: 18th annual Showcase Showdown
description: Big air with a junior rail jam added for the first time. $22,000 in total prizes; $10,000 to the pro men's winner plus a start in the WSSF Monster Energy Shred Show. Presented by Monster Energy, Burton and Vans, with an after-party featuring Anti-Flag. Snowboard Magazine lists the contest date as Saturday 14 March; the Georgia Straight gives 14-15 March.

name: 2026 Sidesurfers Banked Slalom
description: Dates from a third-party events roundup, not from the organiser.

name: 1985 Snoboard Shop North American Snowboarding Championships (first edition)
description: SnowboardQuebec's history page states Ken Achenbach's Snoboard Shop launched the North American Snowboarding Championships in Alberta in 1985 with a $20,000 purse, calling it the first snowboard event held in Canada, and says the series ended in 1988. Venue for 1985 is unconfirmed: the 1987 edition is sourced to Sunshine Village and later accounts describe an annual May long weekend contest there, but the one source naming a 1985 result places the event 'in Calgary'.

name: 1987 Snoboard Shop North American Championships
description: Held on the May long weekend with a $20,000 purse. A photograph of Dave Achenbach from this event ran on the cover of the first issue of TransWorld Snowboarding. Exact dates and the disciplines run were not sourced.

name: 1988 Snoboard Shop North American Snowboarding Championships
description: Norquay's own history says hosting the event put the resort on the cover of TransWorld Snowboarding. SnowboardQuebec's history records 1988 as the final year of the series.
catalog_status_note: Venue changed: Sunshine Village withdrew from hosting mid-season and Mt Norquay took the event on.

name: 2013 Snowboard Jamboree / FIS Snowboarding World Championships
description: The 2013 FIS Snowboarding World Championships were staged at Stoneham on these dates. Ski Canada's 2014 preview describes the 2014 Jamboree as the 9th edition, which places the 2013 festival as the 8th.

name: 9th Snowboard Jamboree
description: Billed as the 9th Snowboard Jamboree and the 15th World Cup held in Quebec. First year the event was sanctioned as a 5-star World Snowboard Tour stop and first year it offered three freestyle World Cup disciplines. Last international snowboard competition before the Sochi 2014 Olympics. Stairsmasters video contest returned.
venue_name: Stoneham Mountain Resort and Quebec City

name: 10th Snowboard Jamboree
description: 10th edition and the 16th FIS Snowboard World Cup held at the festival. Big air on 20 February at Ilot Fleurie in downtown Quebec City, slopestyle on 21 February at Stoneham. About 200 athletes from more than 20 countries. First time 19 women contested big air at a World Cup here. Stairsmasters video contest ran alongside.
catalog_status_note: The halfpipe World Cup scheduled for 22 February at Stoneham was cancelled: organisers cited a significant lack of snow, warm weather and a labour dispute making an FIS-standard pipe impossible.
venue_name: Stoneham Mountain Resort and Ilot Fleurie, Quebec City

name: 2016 Snowboard Jamboree
description: Moved entirely into downtown Quebec City and cut back to a single big air World Cup, carrying both FIS and TTR World Snowboard Tour points. Maxence Parrot worked on the venue build. Programme also included the Stairsmasters video contest and the IF3 film festival. Organisers described 16 years of World Cup racing in the region and seven consecutive World Cups in Quebec City from 2009.

name: 2018 Jamboree Big Air World Cup Finals
description: Listed on Canada Snowboard's 2017-18 domestic calendar as the Jamboree Big Air World Cup Finals.

name: 2019 Jamboree Snowboard and Ski Big Air
description: Listed on Canada Snowboard's 2018-19 domestic calendar as the Jamboree Snowboard and Ski Big Air.

name: SBM BANKED+ 2024
description: Open practice Friday 29 March, competition Saturday 30 March. 150 men and 100 women; entrants had to be 18 or over and resident in Japan. Entry JPY 2,000, JPY 1,000 for JSBA/PSA members.
catalog_status_note: Run as a banked slalom rather than SBM's usual freeride-performance and obstacle-slalom format, because seasonal conditions made it impossible to prepare the standard courses.
venue_name: Yamabiko B Course, Nozawa Onsen Ski Resort

name: 1991 Victoria World Cup Japan
description: Snowboarder/TransWorld 1990s timeline: the Victoria World Cup Japan at Rusutsu, with over one million dollars spent, was 'the richest contest so far'. No dates, format or podium given. This is a single tour stop, not a full season row.

name: Absolut Park Spring Battle 2007
description: Sunday ran as the TTR 3-Star event with qualification runs and finals; skate sessions and a party ran alongside.
catalog_status_note: Saturday's main contest was postponed because of weather and replaced by a Best Trick Session on the last three obstacles.

name: Spring Battle 2025
description: WSF Elite Level Event counting for the World Snowboard Points List, EUR 65,000 prize purse. Riders had several days to film single-take runs with follow-cam filmers (no editing permitted), judged afterwards by an international WSF panel. Snowboard slopestyle on the Absolut Park kicker line; Best Trick Rail open to snowboarders and freeskiers in a dedicated jib park. Award ceremony 14 March at Haus Flachau.

name: Stylewars 007 presented by Oakley
description: Swatch TTR 3-Star. Ran the week after the Garnier Fructis Australian Open at Perisher Blue.

name: Stylewars 2010
description: Billed by the WSF as Australia's biggest Swatch TTR tour event (4-Star), drawing riders from across the southern hemisphere.

name: Stylewars 2011
description: 25 riders. A '28 Stairs' rail jam ran alongside. Scotty James, then 17, led after day one; Gjermund Braaten withdrew injured. The WSF report is dated 23 August 2011 and does not name the resort.
catalog_status_note: Slopestyle scaled back from three days to two.

name: 2026 Sugarloaf Banked Slalom
description: Also referred to as the Mike Baker Banked Slalom. Dates from a third-party events roundup.

name: Suomi Tour 2015
description: Four stops: Vuokatti (7-8 Feb), Ounasvaara (21-22 Feb), Talma (14-15 Mar) and Ruka (9-12 Apr, run as SM15, the Finnish championships). Grom, Rookie and Open categories; EUR 35 entry with an FSA licence covering the three regional events; Burton Riglet park and coaching for parents and non-competing young riders.

name: Swiss Freestyle Snowboard Championships 2014
description: Closing event of the Swiss-Ski Audi Snowboard Series season, and the first time in years that the snowboard freestyle championships were held together with the freeskiers.

name: Tenjin Banked Slalom 2012
description: Listed by the WSF as Japan's banked slalom, roughly 1.5 hours from Tokyo. Earliest edition found.

name: Tenjin Banked Slalom 2015
description: WSF report says the contest had run for three seasons before this one. Organised by former pro rider Yosuke Nishida, director of the TJ brand, on Mt Tanigawa.

name: Tenjin Banked Slalom 2016
description: Heats on 5 March in clear weather, finals over two runs on 6 March. Course deliberately balanced for regular and goofy riders; based out of the Canyons lodge at the resort base. Snowboard brands demoed 2016/17 models alongside.

name: Tenjin Banked Slalom 2017
description: Over 400 people across the two days. Opened with a traditional ceremony praying for safety, reflecting the mountain's avalanche history. Riders received a TBS x Volcom collaboration T-shirt.

name: The Arctic Challenge 1999 (pilot)
description: Pilot project: Terje Haakonsen, Daniel Franck and Oakley invited 12 riders to Norway to test the concept. Halfpipe in Trysil, surfing and freeriding in Lofoten. Terje later described 2014 as '15 years since we did the pilot event'.

name: The Arctic Challenge 2000
description: First full competition: halfpipe, quarterpipe, surf, skate and freeride.

name: The Arctic Challenge 2001
description: Moved south because of weather: halfpipe at Hemsedal, quarterpipe at Holmenkollen in Oslo. Heikki Sorsa set a 9.3 m quarterpipe air record at this event.

name: The Arctic Challenge 2002
catalog_status_note: Cancelled after the sports marketing firm Sportsworld went bankrupt; Terje Haakonsen personally took on the financial obligations.

name: The Arctic Challenge 2004
description: Halfpipe and quarterpipe plus a music and lifestyle programme.

name: The Arctic Challenge 2005
description: Last edition held above the Arctic Circle; from 2006 the event moved to the Oslo area. Show sessions replaced the cancelled contests.
catalog_status_note: Arctic storms forced relocations; the halfpipe and slopestyle were cancelled and only the Tromsø quarterpipe ran, in pouring rain.

name: The Arctic Challenge 2006
description: First edition in Oslo.
catalog_status_note: Major weather delays; scaffolding had to be replaced before the event.

name: The Arctic Challenge 2007
description: Terje Haakonsen set a quarterpipe air record of 9.8 m above the lip, beating Heikki Sorsa's 9.3 m from 2001. Venue not stated in the sources I opened. [QA-corrected: venue and date taken from the cited the-house.com history, which the original row overlooked.]

name: Oakley Arctic Challenge 2008
description: About 7,000 spectators in good weather.

name: Oakley Arctic Challenge 2010
description: TTR 6Star slopestyle. Practice and a downtown Oslo grand opening on Thursday 4 March, semi-finals Saturday 6 March, finals Sunday 7 March; capacity 4,000. Course shaper Claes Hoegstrom. Peetu Piiroinen's win here secured the Swatch TTR world title.

name: Oakley Arctic Challenge 2011
description: 6Star slopestyle with 30 men and 16 women and a USD 100,000 purse; qualification from the TTR ranking (top 20 men, top 10 women after the Burton European Open), qualifying events and wildcards. Staged as the trial run for the 2012 World Snowboarding Championships.

name: The Arctic Challenge 2013
description: Main snowboard event on 9 March 2013, with a halfpipe competition (snowboard and freestyle ski) five days earlier; the volunteer call covered 6-13 March. Start date not stated explicitly.

name: The Arctic Challenge 2014
description: Rider-designed format: 12 riders arrived 11 March and had the pipe from 12-15 March to decide the arena and contest format themselves, with the public event on Saturday 15 March. Judged on skill, amplitude and creativity rather than a standard run score. 15 years after the 1999 pilot.

name: The BRITS 2009 (20th birthday)
description: 20th birthday edition, billed by the WSF as Europe's longest established winter snowsports festival. Hosted the British Snowboard and Freeski Championships across kids, rookie, pro and Olympian fields; a skiercross ran alongside.

name: The BRITS 2023
description: First return to Scotland in 32 years. Ran as the TSA British Snowboard Championships alongside the Ellis Brigham British Freeski Championships. Cairngorm built the first British halfpipe in 1991.

name: 1st Toyota Big Air
description: Inaugural edition. Editions were normally held around 11 February.

name: 6th Toyota Big Air
description: Olympic year; the Japanese Wikipedia notes that in Olympic years the date shifted to late January or late February.

name: 10th Toyota Big Air
description: Olympic year.

name: 11th Toyota Big Air
description: The Makomanai open-air stadium carried the Sekisui Heim naming rights from 2007.

name: 14th Toyota Big Air
description: Olympic year.

name: 15th Toyota Big Air
description: Last edition held outdoors at Makomanai.

name: 16th Toyota Big Air
description: Moved indoors to the Sapporo Dome as a 'full model change', with a 36 m temporary in-run scaffold.

name: 18th Toyota Big Air
description: Final edition. The organising office announced on 30 September 2014 that the event would not continue. Date of 23 February 2014 taken from the English Wikipedia article; the Japanese article gives no per-edition dates.

name: 2002/03 TTR Pro Snowboarding Series season
description: First TTR season: nine events worldwide with the Arctic Challenge as the final stop, each event awarding one TTR Medallion and an Arctic Challenge invite. No women's tour until 2005/06. Events: Nissan X-Trail Jam, Nokia Air & Style, O'Neill SB Jam, Burton European Open, Champs Open, Vans Triple Crown of Snowboarding, The Battle, Quiksilver Slopestyle Pro, US Open.

name: 2003/04 TTR Pro Snowboarding Series season
description: Same nine events as the previous season; the nine TTR medallion winners were invited to the Arctic Challenge, again the tour final.

name: 2004/05 TTR World Snowboard Tour season
description: Season edition rows use the calendar year the season ended. The Arctic Challenge's own 2005 site published the 2004/2005 TTR Tour standings, with Andy Finch as overall champion, which confirms the season ran.

name: 2005/06 TTR World Snowboard Tour season
description: Introduction of the 1-6Star tier system, the TTR ranking system, the first TTR website (ttrworldtour.com) and the official Women's Tour. 67 events in total. The TTR World Ranking list launched 5 December 2005 and the first-ever TTR World Tour Champions were crowned at the US Open.

name: 2006/07 TTR World Snowboard Tour season
description: First season with a dedicated women's tour, announced 24 October 2006. WSF described a provisional women's calendar of over 20 events offering more than 30 possible results, kicking off with the Burton Abominable Snow Jam at Mt Hood in July 2006 and ending at the Roxy Chicken Jam Finals in Park City, 22-25 March 2007. The Billabong Pro Junior in Australia and the Burton Australian Open were cancelled for poor snow.

name: 2007/08 Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour season
description: Introduction of a $250,000 end-of-season prize purse. 176 results registered across four formats from events in 27 nations; 3,417 riders (2,706 men, 711 women) from 41 nations ranked.

name: 2008/09 Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour season
description: First of Peetu Piiroinen's three consecutive men's overall titles, per Guinness World Records.

name: 2009/10 Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour season
description: Second of Peetu Piiroinen's three consecutive men's overall titles; WSF reported he secured the Swatch TTR world title by winning the Oakley Arctic Challenge in March 2010.

name: 2010/11 Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour season
description: Third of Peetu Piiroinen's three consecutive men's overall titles, per Guinness World Records.

name: 2011/12 World Snowboard Tour season
description: TTR's 10th anniversary season. Highlight was the inaugural World Snowboarding Championships at Oslo Vinterpark in February 2012, developed and owned by TTR and the World Snowboard Federation and run as a 6Star tour event - the first world championships organised by snowboarders since 1999. The Burton European Open was postponed to March, making WCS qualification difficult.

name: 2012/13 World Snowboard Tour season
description: First season under the new name. TTR announced on 2-4 July 2012 that the TTR World Tour would be called the World Snowboard Tour from the 2012/13 season; TTR president Reto Lamm said the tour then covered around 350 events across five continents. Headline events named in the announcement were Air & Style Beijing and Innsbruck, Burton European and US Open, O'Neill Evolution Davos and The Arctic Challenge Oslo.

name: 2013/14 World Snowboard Tour season
description: Season in which the six star tiers were replaced by four event categories: Regional, National, International and Elite.

name: 2014/15 World Snowboard Tour season
description: First season under the new tour concept agreed at the May 2014 General Assembly in Barcelona: six star tiers replaced by four categories (Regional, National, International, Elite), with the Elite events forming the WST Pro Series. Titles were awarded in slopestyle and halfpipe only, at the Burton US Open on 8 March 2015.

name: 2016/17 World Snowboard Tour season
description: TTR Pro Snowboarding restricted access to the World Snowboard Points List in January 2017 to force the snowboard industry to fund it. The merger with the WSF was announced 25 May 2017; from the 2017/18 season the merged organisation offered direct membership and the World Snowboard Tour brand ceased to exist.
catalog_status_note: Final season before the tour brand was retired.

name: 1982 National Snowsurfing Championships
description: Organised by Paul Graves. Doug Bouton won. Burton's own history page opens the US Open lineage with this event; the PSIA-AASI archive treats it as a separate contest from the National Snowboarding Championships Jake Burton Carpenter organised at Snow Valley the following year. Recorded here as the first row of the lineage with the dispute unresolved.

name: 1983 National Snowboarding Championships
description: No lift access; competitors hiked the hill. Andy Coghlan won men's slalom and downhill. Several sources describe this, not 1982, as the first edition of what became the US Open, and Burton's own later edition numbering (2002 = 20th, 2009 = 27th, 2012 = 30th, 2020 = 38th) counts from 1983.

name: 1984 National Snowboarding Championships
description: Final year at Snow Valley. Andy Coghlan repeated in slalom and downhill.

name: 1985 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: First year at Stratton Mountain and the year the event was formally called the US Open Snowboarding Championships. Riders began wearing speed suits. Tom Sims won men's slalom; Andy Coghlan defended the downhill.

name: 1986 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Over 200 competitors in the pre-qualifiers. Andy Coghlan won slalom and downhill again.

name: 1987 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Craig Kelly won the men's slalom.

name: 1988 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Halfpipe debuted at the US Open and was immediately treated as the benchmark for competition pipes. Craig Kelly took the overall title. An ice storm preceded the event.

name: 1989 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Last year the downhill was run. Craig Kelly won the Overall title. [QA-corrected: the cited sources say halfpipe DEBUTED at the 1989 US Open and that Kelly took the Overall title; the earlier claim of a second consecutive halfpipe title was unsupported. The downhill discipline was uncited and has been removed.]

name: 1990 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Terje Haakonsen's US Open halfpipe debut. Craig Kelly won, against a field including Shaun Palmer and Jeff Brushie.

name: 1991 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Crowd and competitor numbers roughly doubled. Inverts ridden in competition for the first time. Janna Meyen won the women's halfpipe over Tina Basich.

name: 1992 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Terje Haakonsen won the men's halfpipe; Tricia Byrnes won the women's.

name: 1993 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Fresh snow and clear skies. Terje Haakonsen took a second consecutive halfpipe title on his new Burton pro model.

name: 1994 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Shannon Dunn and Todd Richards won the halfpipes. Terje Haakonsen sat out with an ankle injury.

name: 1995 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Big air debuted at the US Open. Terje Haakonsen won a third halfpipe title. Victoria Jealouse won the women's super-G, recorded here as discipline 'other' because super-G is not in the Linestry discipline vocabulary.

name: 1996 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Held in the season snowboarding's inclusion in the 1998 Nagano Olympics was announced. Peter Line and Cara-Beth Burnside won big air; Jimi Scott and Satu Jarvela won halfpipe.

name: 1997 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Reported crowd of over 10,000 for the halfpipe. Todd Richards edged Terje Haakonsen; Barrett Christy won the women's pipe.

name: 1998 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Remembered as 'the Year of the Mist' for heavy fog. Boardercross debuted. Rob Kingwill won the men's halfpipe; Nicola Thost, the 1998 Olympic champion, won the women's. Mike Michalchuk's back-to-back 1620s are cited by Burton as an early double-cork-era moment.

name: 1999 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Ross Powers won the men's halfpipe with McTwists and 900s; Nicola Thost won the women's for a second consecutive year.

name: 2000 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: First superpipe at the US Open, reported as roughly 300 feet long with 15-foot walls. Guillaume Morisset and Natasza Zurek won for Canada. Recorded as halfpipe; the pipe event was run as a superpipe from this year.

name: 2001 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Danny Kass won the men's halfpipe, narrowly over Vermont's Abe Teter. Natasza Zurek took a second consecutive women's title.

name: 2002 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Held a month after the Salt Lake City Olympics, with a reported 30,000-plus spectators. Kelly Clark won quarterpipe and halfpipe; Danny Kass defended the men's halfpipe. First Tracks called it the 20th year of the competition, which counts from 1983. [v0.2: MountainZone reports the first US Open slopestyle finals on 17 March 2002, with both podiums; discipline list corrected.]

name: 2003 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: First rail jam at the US Open, won by Travis Rice; first live television broadcast; Philips became the first title sponsor. Ross Powers won the halfpipe, Gretchen Bleiler the women's, Shaun White the slopestyle. MountainZone's contemporaneous slopestyle report is dated 2003-03-15; full event dates not sourced. [v0.3 archive: Open Championships of Snowboarding 2003 calendar: "Mar 11 - 16, 2003 Stratton, VT". The usopen03 schedule page confirms Rail Jam final Friday 14 March, halfpipe finals Saturday 15 March, slopestyle finals Sunday 16 March.] [v0.3 archive: Open Championships of Snowboarding 2003 calendar: "Mar 11 - 16, 2003 Stratton, VT". The usopen03 schedule page confirms Rail Jam final Friday 14 March, halfpipe finals Saturday 15 March, slopestyle finals Sunday 16 March.]

name: 2004 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Women rode the rail jam for the first time; Leanne Pelosi won. Danny Kass won the halfpipe and the overall title; Kelly Clark won the women's halfpipe. Priscilla Levac and Jake Blauvelt won slopestyle. [v0.3 archive: 2004 Open Championships of Snowboarding calendar: "Philips US Open March 16-21, 2004 Stratton, VT USA".] [v0.3 archive: 2004 Open Championships of Snowboarding calendar: "Philips US Open March 16-21, 2004 Stratton, VT USA".]

name: 2005 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Danny Kass became the first rider to win four US Open halfpipe titles. Janna Meyen won her first title since 1991. [v0.3 archive: Open Championships of Snowboarding calendar: "US Open Mar. 14-20, 2005 Stratton, VT USA". The usopen05 schedule page runs Monday March 14th (practice) to Sunday March 20th.] [v0.3 archive: Open Championships of Snowboarding calendar: "US Open Mar. 14-20, 2005 Stratton, VT USA". The usopen05 schedule page runs Monday March 14th (practice) to Sunday March 20th.]

name: 2006 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Shaun White won halfpipe and slopestyle. The quarterpipe was revived, won by Danny Davis and Hana Beaman. White and Beaman took Most Valuable Rider awards. [v0.3 archive: Open Championships of Snowboarding calendar: "US Open March 14-19, 2006 Stratton, VT USA".] [v0.3 archive: Open Championships of Snowboarding calendar: "US Open March 14-19, 2006 Stratton, VT USA".]

name: 2007 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Marked by Burton as the 25th anniversary. Shaun White and Torah Bright won the first Burton Global Open Series championship titles, USD 100,000 each. Kelly Clark won a third halfpipe title; Travis Rice and Jamie Anderson won slopestyle. [v0.3 archive: Burton Global Open Series press release: "US Open March 12-18, 2007 Stratton, VT, USA".] [v0.3 archive: Burton Global Open Series press release: "US Open March 12-18, 2007 Stratton, VT, USA".]

name: 2008 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Total prize purse reported at USD 471,500. Rated 6Star on the Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour. Slopestyle finals ran 2008-03-21 (Shaun White and Kjersti Buaas) with halfpipe finals the following day; the event's start date was not sourced. Cheryl Maas and Tim Humphreys won big air.

name: 2009 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Closing event of the 2008/09 Burton Global Open Series; dates as announced in the series calendar. AlpineZone called it the 27th US Open. Danny Kass won a record fifth halfpipe title; Torah Bright won a third. Chas Guldemond and Kjersti Buaas won slopestyle. A best trick contest and a junior jam were also run, recorded as 'other'.

name: 2010 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Halfpipe finals ran 2010-03-20 in a slushy pipe; full event dates not sourced. Kazuhiro Kokubo won his first halfpipe title and Kelly Clark became the first woman to win four. Mikkel Bang and Sina Candrian won slopestyle. [v0.3 archive: Burton Global Open Series calendar listed the US Open as March 16-21, 2010. Refines the existing 2010-03 value.] [v0.3 archive: Burton Global Open Series calendar listed the US Open as March 16-21, 2010. Refines the existing 2010-03 value.] [v0.3 QA: the archive citation was a Flash-only page containing no dates and has been removed. The dates rest on the live-web sources.]

name: 2011 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Kazuhiro Kokubo won a second consecutive halfpipe title and dedicated it to tsunami-hit Japan. Kelly Clark won a fifth consecutive halfpipe title and her first Burton Global Open Series championship. Eric Willett and Enni Rukajarvi won their first slopestyle titles.

name: 2012 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: Last US Open at Stratton after 28 editions there. Hit by a freak snowstorm. Shaun White won halfpipe; Elena Hight ended Kelly Clark's streak; Seb Toots and Jamie Anderson won slopestyle; Chas Guldemond and Kjersti Buaas won The Jam. A veterans' race, the Washed Up Cup, was run on the Friday night.

name: 2013 US Open Snowboarding Championships
description: First US Open at Vail after 28 years in Vermont. Over USD 340,000 in prize money. Mark McMorris won his first slopestyle title, Spencer O'Brien the women's; Shaun White won the halfpipe with 14-year-old Ayumu Hirano second.

name: 32nd Burton US Open (2014)
description: Slopestyle finals 2014-03-07, halfpipe finals 2014-03-08. Mark McMorris won a second consecutive slopestyle; Jamie Anderson won the women's; Kelly Clark won the halfpipe.

name: 33rd Burton US Open (2015)
description: Yuki Kadono won men's slopestyle with back-to-back triple cork 1620s, reported as a competition first. Jamie Anderson won a fourth slopestyle title; Kelly Clark won an eighth halfpipe title; Taku Hiraoka won the men's halfpipe.

name: 34th Burton US Open (2016)
description: USD 343,000 prize purse. Shaun White returned to the halfpipe podium; 15-year-old Chloe Kim won her first halfpipe title. Jamie Anderson and Kyle Mack won slopestyle. Junior jam halfpipe on 2016-03-01.

name: 35th Burton US Open (2017)
description: Anna Gasser won her first title in women's slopestyle; Mark McMorris won the men's. Shaun White and Chloe Kim defended their halfpipe titles. Junior jam halfpipe for riders 14 and under.

name: 36th Burton US Open (2018)
description: First post-PyeongChang edition. Zoi Sadowski-Synnott and Red Gerard won slopestyle; Maddie Mastro and Scotty James won halfpipe.

name: 37th Burton US Open (2019)
description: Halfpipe and slopestyle for men and women plus a junior jam for riders under 15.

name: 38th Burton US Open (2020)
description: The last US Open held. Run about four months after Jake Burton Carpenter's death and dedicated to him. USD 373,000 prize purse. Junior jam halfpipe 2020-02-25; slopestyle finals 2020-02-28; halfpipe finals 2020-02-29.

name: 2021 Burton US Open (cancelled)
description: Scheduled for 2021-03-01 to 2021-03-06 and cancelled. Burton later confirmed the US Open would not be returning to Vail and pointed to the new Burton Mystery Series, intended to be hosted in a different country each time. Vail had invested USD 490,000 in the 2020 event and did not budget for 2022.
catalog_status_note: Cancelled; the event did not return to Vail afterwards.

name: 2021 Toyota U.S. Grand Prix, Copper Mountain (halfpipe World Cup)
description: FIS reported the snowboard halfpipe World Cup at this Toyota U.S. Grand Prix on 14 December 2021. Only the halfpipe date was confirmed; the full run of the Grand Prix week at Copper was not established.

name: 1990 USASA National Championships
description: Snowboarder/TransWorld 1990s timeline: February 1990 at Snow Valley, California; a severe snowstorm stranded competitors and USASA president Chuck Allen led the rescue. No podium found. City given as Running Springs, California (Snow Valley's town) - not confirmed in the sources opened. Not to be confused with Snow Valley, Vermont, which hosted the 1983 and 1984 National Snowboarding Championships.

name: 2023 USASA National Championships
description: Snowboard championships ran March 31-April 6, 2023; the freeski championships followed April 8-12, 2023. About 1,500 snowboard and freeski competitors attended in total.

name: 2025 USASA National Championships
description: Full championship window March 28-April 9, 2025; snowboard competition March 30-April 3 and freeski April 6-9. Daily formats are confirmed nightly at the Team Captains Meeting.

name: 2026 USASA National Championships
description: Dates from an events listing, not from USASA directly; disciplines for this specific edition not confirmed from the organiser.

name: 1999/2000 Vans Triple Crown of Snowboarding
description: Three stops: Breckenridge, Colorado 3-5 December 1999 (boardercross, big air with a USD 10,000 winner's cheque, halfpipe); Mount Seymour, British Columbia 14-16 January 2000 (snowboard cross, halfpipe); Sierra-at-Tahoe, California 25-27 February 2000 (halfpipe). Overall titles to Ross Powers and Ina Poetzl, with a USD 10,000 overall prize.

name: 10th Vans Waengl Taengl presented by G-SHOCK
description: Tenth-anniversary edition, a week-long 'contest-ival' billed as the world's largest snowboard team competition, with team skate, open-air concerts, parties and art installations alongside. Organised by the Aesthetiker.

name: Waengl Taengl 2013 (not held)
description: The crew said they would instead focus on youth development and new event formats.
catalog_status_note: The Aesthetiker announced a break from producing the event in 2013. Club president Steve Gruber: 'we felt we needed time to look at how we could step it up again to guarantee the next edition of the Waengl is kick arse, not an anti-climax.'

name: 1989 WestBeach Classic (first edition)
description: First edition. Sources disagree on venue and format: Whistler Blackcomb's own 60th anniversary timeline says the WestBeach Classic launched at Blackcomb in 1989 and that Ross Rebagliati won the halfpipe and landed the cover of TransWorld Snowboarding; photographer Dano Pendygrasse recalls the first event as a big air at Cypress Mountain. Venue left null pending a contemporaneous source.

name: 1997 WestBeach Invitational Big Air
description: Run inside the 1997 World Ski & Snowboard Festival (4-13 April 1997). Over 8,000 spectators at the base of Whistler Mountain. Exact contest date not sourced.

name: 2000 WestBeach Classic
description: Final edition. Moved out of the World Ski & Snowboard Festival to the May long weekend. Reported in 2001 by Pique Newsmagazine as the last running.

name: 2001 WestBeach Classic
description: The Masters Group organised both the WestBeach Classic and the World Snowboarding Championship.
catalog_status_note: Not held. WestBeach Sports redirected its funding to sponsor the World Snowboarding Championship instead; company president Steve Dewar told Pique the brand opportunity was 'too good to pass up'.

name: 2001 FIS Snowboard World Cup, Whistler
description: Pique Newsmagazine's 2001 year in sports records snowboard cross, two halfpipes, alpine and big air over these dates, with Guillaume Morisset taking a bronze, Natasza Zurek a silver and Jasey-Jay Anderson a silver in parallel giant slalom. Belongs to the 2001-02 season.

name: 2019 Halfpipe Rodeo FIS Ski & Snowboard World Cup
description: Announced by Canada Snowboard in November 2018 and listed on its 2018-19 domestic calendar.

name: 2020 FIS Freestyle Ski and Snowboard World Cups, Calgary
description: Part of a season in which Canada hosted a World Cup in every snowboard discipline.

name: 2008-09 Winter Dew Tour, Stop 1: Breckenridge
description: Opening stop of the inaugural Winter Dew Tour. Men's and women's snowboard and freeski slopestyle and superpipe; $1.5 million purse across the three stops; Dew Cup awarded to season champions. Belongs to the 2008-09 season.

name: 2008-09 Winter Dew Tour, Stop 2: Mount Snow
description: Second stop of the 2008-09 season.

name: 2008-09 Winter Dew Tour, Stop 3: Northstar-at-Tahoe
description: Season finale of the 2008-09 season. [QA-corrected: end_date removed, not carried by either citation.]

name: 2009-10 Winter Dew Tour, Stop 1: Breckenridge
description: Opening stop of the 2009-10 season. The season article lists only men's superpipe and men's slopestyle for this stop; whether women's fields ran here is unconfirmed.

name: 2009-10 Winter Dew Tour, Stop 2: Snowbasin
description: Second stop of the 2009-10 season; men's and women's superpipe and slopestyle.

name: 2009-10 Winter Dew Tour, Stop 3: Mount Snow
description: Third stop of the 2009-10 season; men's and women's superpipe and slopestyle.

name: 2009-10 Winter Dew Tour, Toyota Championship: Northstar-at-Tahoe
description: Listed as the season finale of the 2009-10 Winter Dew Tour. No dates found; year assigned to 2010 on the assumption the finale followed the February Mount Snow stop, which is NOT sourced. See open_questions.

name: 2010-11 Winter Dew Tour, Stop 1: Breckenridge
description: Opening stop of the 2010-11 season; new 22-foot superpipe at Breckenridge.

name: 2010-11 Winter Dew Tour, Stop 2: Killington
description: Vermont stop moved from Mount Snow to Killington for the 2010-11 season.

name: 2010-11 Winter Dew Tour, Toyota Championship: Snowbasin
description: Season finale of the 2010-11 season; Dew Cup awarded.

name: 2011-12 Winter Dew Tour, Stop 1: Breckenridge
description: Opening stop of the 2011-12 season.

name: 2011-12 Winter Dew Tour, Stop 2: Killington
description: Second stop of the 2011-12 season.

name: 2011-12 Winter Dew Tour, Toyota Championship: Snowbasin
description: Season finale of the 2011-12 season; last multi-stop Winter Dew Tour season.

name: Dew Tour Mountain Championships 2012 (Breckenridge)
description: First season under the restructured single-winter-stop format ('the lone Winter Dew Tour stop'). A Main Street rail jam ran alongside the mountain events (recorded as 'jib').

name: Dew Tour Mountain Championships 2013 (Breckenridge)
description: Announced as the Mountain Championships leg of the three-stop 2013 Dew Tour (Ocean City, San Francisco, Breckenridge). Snowboard discipline list not confirmed.

name: Dew Tour Mountain Championships 2014 (Breckenridge)
description: Men's and women's snowboard slopestyle and superpipe plus men's Snowboard Streetstyle (recorded as 'jib'). Described as the seventh straight year at Breckenridge. Dates from a secondary event listing, not an organiser release.

name: Dew Tour Breckenridge 2015
description: Men's and women's snowboard superpipe and slopestyle finals plus a Snowboard Streetstyle final (recorded as 'jib').

name: Dew Tour Breckenridge 2016
description: Run in Breckenridge's Freeway Terrain Park. Individual men's and women's slopestyle and pipe, plus a new brand Team Challenge format (recorded as 'team'). First winter edition under TEN: The Enthusiast Network ownership.

name: Dew Tour Breckenridge 2017
description: Men's and women's snowboard slopestyle and superpipe (a U.S. Ski & Snowboard Olympic qualifying event), a combined ski/snowboard Streetstyle (recorded as 'jib') and a Team Challenge on a modified superpipe/jib/jump course (recorded as 'team').

name: Dew Tour Breckenridge 2018
description: Eleventh and final Breckenridge edition. Men's and women's ski and snowboard slopestyle and halfpipe, a para snowboard competition (recorded as 'other'), a 12-brand Team Challenge, and a Streetstyle jam in downtown Breckenridge (recorded as 'jib').

name: Dew Tour Copper Mountain 2020
description: First Copper Mountain edition after 11 years at Breckenridge. Men's and women's halfpipe, slopestyle in Copper's Central Park, para snowboard (recorded as 'other') and the Team Challenge. Note the calendar-year gap: the previous edition was December 2018, so no Winter Dew Tour was held in calendar 2019.

name: Dew Tour Copper Mountain 2021
description: Beijing 2022 Olympic qualifying event. DATE CONFLICT: U.S. Ski & Snowboard gives December 15-19, 2021; Summit Daily's preview gives December 16-19. More than 200 athletes from 17 countries in ski and snowboard superpipe, slopestyle and adaptive snowboard slalom (recorded as 'other').

name: Dew Tour Copper Mountain 2023
description: Based in Copper's Center Village. Men's and women's ski and snowboard superpipe and slopestyle, a Super Streetstyle (recorded as 'jib') and superpipe high air / best trick jams (recorded as 'other'). No Winter Dew Tour was held in calendar 2022.

name: Dew Tour Copper Mountain 2024
description: Final Winter Dew Tour. Dates are as stated in the headlines of the Dew Tour and PR Newswire announcements; neither page body could be retrieved (dewtour.com blocked the fetcher via robots.txt). Discipline list not confirmed. Dew Tour announced in 2024 that the winter event would not return from 2025 onward.

name: 2009 New Zealand Winter Games
description: Inaugural edition: 7 sports, 51 events.

name: 2011 New Zealand Winter Games
description: Expanded to 9 sports. Included a WSF Para-Snowboard World Cup at Cardrona Alpine Resort.

name: 2015 New Zealand Winter Games
description: 5 sports.

name: 2017 New Zealand Winter Games
description: Last edition of the biennial era; the Games went annual from 2018.

name: 2018 Winter Games NZ
description: First annual edition.

name: 2019 Winter Games NZ
description: 5 sports.

name: 2020 Winter Games NZ
description: Run in the new Obsidian format for New Zealand athletes only.

name: 2021 Winter Games NZ (cancelled)
catalog_status_note: Cancelled because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

name: 2022 Winter Games NZ
description: International athletes returned; 4 sports.

name: 2023 Winter Games NZ
description: 14 events across alpine, freeride and freestyle park and pipe. Hosted the FIS Park & Pipe Junior World Championships. The International Obsidian Challenge, an athlete-focused team event for freeski and snowboard, ran 9-16 September as a new addition.
venue_name: Cardrona Alpine Resort, Coronet Peak, The Remarkables

name: 2024 Winter Games NZ
description: Final edition. FIS World Cup events resumed; 4 sports. The Games were wound up on 23 January 2025.

name: Winter X Games I (1997)
description: First edition. Snowboard Magazine's history names Snow Summit, Big Bear as the site and lists slopestyle, big air, snowboarder X and halfpipe, noting the pipe was 12 feet tall. Non-snowboard disciplines included ice climbing, snow mountain bike racing and shovel racing.

name: Winter X Games II (1998)
description: Aspen Daily News gives January 1998; no exact dates found. Freeskiing, snowmobile SnoCross and skiboarding added to the overall programme. Discipline list is from a Snowboard Magazine results retrospective that tracked only halfpipe, slopestyle and big air; whether snowboarder X ran is unconfirmed.

name: Winter X Games III (1999)
description: Aspen Daily News gives January 1999; no exact dates found. Same caveat on the discipline list as 1998.

name: Winter X Games IV (2000)
description: First East Coast Winter X Games. Aspen Daily News reports snowboard SuperPipe added this year and the pipe wall height raised to 15 feet. Record attendance reported as 83,500.

name: Winter X Games V (2001)
description: No exact dates found in any source opened. Moto X Big Air debuted at this edition.

name: Winter X Games VI (2002)
description: First Aspen edition; Buttermilk has hosted every year since. DATE CONFLICT, left null: the Wikipedia X Games article gives February 1-5, 2002 while the Aspen Daily News history gives January 17-20, 2002. Snowboard Magazine's retrospective suggests big air was not run for snowboard between 2002 and 2006, but this is unconfirmed, so disciplines are left null.

name: Winter X Games VII (2003)
description: Dates as given by the Wikipedia X Games article; not cross-checked against an organiser source. Disciplines not confirmed.

name: Winter X Games VIII (2004)
description: Disciplines not confirmed by a source opened.

name: Winter X Games IX (2005)
description: Snowboard events: men's and women's snowboard cross, slopestyle and SuperPipe. No snowboard big air this year.

name: Winter X Games X (2006)
description: Disciplines not confirmed by a source opened.

name: Winter X Games XI (2007)
description: Men's Snowboard Best Trick added this year (recorded as 'other'); plus men's and women's snowboard cross, slopestyle and SuperPipe.

name: Winter X Games XII (2008)
description: Men's Snowboard Big Air returns to the programme alongside men's and women's snowboard cross, slopestyle and SuperPipe.

name: Winter X Games XIII (2009)
description: Men's big air, men's and women's superpipe, slopestyle and snowboarder X.

name: Winter X Games XIV (2010)
description: Held two weeks before the 2010 Winter Olympics. Snowboard Best Trick recorded as 'other'. Whether big air had a women's field this year is unconfirmed.

name: Winter X Games XV (2011)
description: DATE CONFLICT: the Winter X Games XV article states January 26-30, 2011; the Wikipedia X Games summary table gives January 27-30. Used the edition article. Programme included Snowboard Street (recorded as 'jib') and Snowboard Best Method (recorded as 'other'). Torstein Horgmo landed the first triple cork in competition in snowboard big air at this edition.

name: Winter X Games XVI (2012)
description: Snowboard Street recorded as 'jib'.

name: Winter X Games XVII (2013)
description: Snowboard Street recorded as 'jib'. No snowboarder X listed for this edition. A separate Winter X Games Europe edition ran at Tignes in March 2013.

name: Winter X Games XIX (2015)
description: DATE CONFLICT: the Winter X Games XIX article states January 21-25, 2015; the Wikipedia X Games summary table gives January 22-25. Used the edition article. Programme included an adaptive snowboarder X event.

name: Winter X Games XX (2016)
description: Event headings on the edition article: men's/women's SlopeStyle, men's Big Air, men's/women's SuperPipe, men's/women's snowboarder X and men's Snowboarder X Adaptive. This is the last edition at which snowboarder X appears in the confirmed event list.

name: Winter X Games XXI (2017)
description: Men's and women's big air, slopestyle and SuperPipe, plus a Special Olympics Unified Snowboarding final (recorded as 'other'). No snowboarder X listed.

name: Winter X Games XXII (2018)
description: Special Olympics Unified Snowboard was run as a dual slalom.

name: Winter X Games XXIII (2019)
description: The edition article states eight snowboarding events but does not head them consistently. Sources disagree on whether Knuckle Huck debuted here (2019) or in 2020, and on whether a snowboard boardercross was run; both are left out pending a checkable results page. See open_questions.

name: Winter X Games XXIV (2020)
description: DATE CONFLICT, left null: the Wikipedia X Games summary table gives January 23-26, 2020, the Winter X Games XXIV article gives 22-26 January 2020. Programme included a men's Rail Jam, a men's Knuckle Huck (recorded as 'other') and a Special Olympics Unified Snowboarding event.

name: Winter X Games XXV (2021)
description: Held without spectators in the COVID-19 era per contemporaneous coverage (not verified here). Knuckle Huck recorded as 'other'; the edition article lists both a men's and a women's Knuckle Huck, which conflicts with reporting that women's Knuckle Huck debuted in 2024. See open_questions.

name: Winter X Games XXVI (2022)
description: Knuckle Huck recorded as 'other'.

name: Winter X Games XXVII (2023)
description: Knuckle Huck recorded as 'other'.

name: Winter X Games XXVIII (2024)
description: Women's Knuckle Huck reported as added to the X Games programme for the first time this year (recorded as 'other').

name: Winter X Games XXIX (2025)
description: Dates confirmed by both the Wikipedia X Games table and the xgames.com past-events listing. Discipline list not confirmed; xgames.com results for this edition are at https://www.xgames.com/results/?event_id=1201 but that page did not render its archive when fetched.

name: Winter X Games XXX (2026)
description: Listed on xgames.com past-events as 'Aspen 2026, January 23-25, 2026'. Discipline list not confirmed and no results URL was published on the past-events page at time of research.

name: Winter X Games Europe 2010 (Tignes)
description: First X Games competition held outside the United States. Men's and women's snowboard slopestyle and superpipe.

name: Winter X Games Europe 2011 (Tignes)
description: Men's and women's snowboard slopestyle and superpipe.

name: Winter X Games Europe 2012 (Tignes)
description: Men's and women's snowboard slopestyle and superpipe.

name: Winter X Games Europe 2013 (Tignes)
description: Final Tignes edition; ESPN cut the event after this year, citing the economics of its international stops. Dates are as stated in the Winter X Games XVII article and not cross-checked against an organiser source. Iouri Podladtchikov landed the first cab double cork 1440 in men's snowboard superpipe at a 2013 X Games edition.

name: 2012 Winter Youth Olympic Games
description: First Winter Youth Olympic Games. Four snowboarding medal events (boys' and girls' halfpipe and slopestyle); 60 competitors from 24 nations. Venue and date detail from the English Wikipedia article, which did not expose citation URLs in the fetch - Olympedia edition id for the 2012 Winter YOG was not located.

name: 2016 Winter Youth Olympic Games
description: Snowboard cross added for boys and girls, plus a mixed team snowboard/ski cross. 79 competitors from 32 nations. Venue and date detail from the English Wikipedia article, which did not expose citation URLs in the fetch - Olympedia edition id for the 2016 Winter YOG was not located. [v0.2: Olympedia lists only six snowboard events at Lillehammer 2016; the mixed-NOC team cross is filed outside snowboarding.]
venue_name: Kanthaugen Freestyle Arena, Lillehammer and Hafjell, Oyer

name: 2020 Winter Youth Olympic Games
description: Eight snowboarding medal events: slopestyle, cross, halfpipe and big air for boys and girls.
venue_name: Leysin Park & Pipe, Leysin and Villars Winter Park, Villars

name: 2024 Winter Youth Olympic Games
description: Nine snowboarding medal events; mixed team cross added. Dates given are the full Games window recorded by Olympedia, not the first and last day of snowboarding competition specifically.

name: Volkl World Rookie Fest 2008, Ischgl
description: Over 50 international competitors. Earliest Ischgl edition found in the WSF archive.

name: 2012 Protest World Rookie Final, Ischgl
description: Prizes valued at EUR 30,000.

name: Völkl World Rookie Finals 2015
description: 3Star TTR event where the World Rookie Champion titles were awarded. Exact dates not given in the source.

name: 2017 World Rookie Finals, Kitzsteinhorn
description: First World Rookie Finals at the Kitzsteinhorn. Climax of a 2016/17 World Rookie Tour season of eleven qualifying events across Chile, Australia, Bulgaria, Scandinavia, the Alps, Japan and North America. Programme included social dinners, workshops and a final party alongside the contests.

name: World Rookie Snowboard Finals 2024
description: Confirmed only by a WSF news item dated 27 March 2024; venue and dates not established in this pass.

name: World Rookie Snowboard Finals 2025
description: Reported by WSF on 8 April 2025. Exact dates not established in this pass.

name: 2014/15 World Rookie Tour season
description: Eleven-stop season: South America Rookie Fest, Valle Nevado, Chile (Aug 2014); Australian Rookie Fest, Thredbo (Aug 2014); Iceripper Rookie Fest, Laax (Jan 2015); WSF World Rookie Fest, Livigno (Jan 2015); Bulgarian Rookie Fest, Pamporovo (Jan-Feb 2015); Transilvania Rookie Fest, Arena Platos, Romania (Feb 2015); Hellas Rookie Fest, Greece (Feb 2015); Trentino Rookie Fest, Monte Bondone (Feb-Mar 2015); Oslo Rookie Fest, Oslo Vinterpark (Feb-Mar 2015); Indy Park Rookie Fest, Nekoma, Japan (Mar 2015); and the 3Star Völkl World Rookie Finals, Ischgl (Apr 2015). Rookies were riders born 1997-1999, Groms 2000 and later. Events counted towards the TTR World Snowboard Tour.

name: Livigno World Rookie Fest 2024 (19th edition)
description: Recorded here as a stop rather than a full season row. Presentation Sunday 14 January, rail jam at the Snowpark20 city park in central Livigno on the Monday afternoon, finals at Mottolino Snowpark on Tuesday 16 January. Described as the nineteenth edition, which implies a first edition in 2006.

name: 1996 World Ski & Snowboard Festival (inaugural)
description: Inaugural festival, directed by Doug Perry. Ten days, 22 competitions, about 1,500 athletes. Consolidated existing spring events including the WestBeach Classic, the Whistler Cup and the Couloir Ski Race Extreme, and added a snowboard museum exhibit and around a dozen bands. First joint marketing initiative between the two rival mountains and the Whistler Resort Association.
venue_name: Whistler Village, Whistler Mountain and Blackcomb Mountain

name: 1997 World Ski & Snowboard Festival
description: Over 2,000 athletes. More than 8,000 spectators at the WestBeach Invitational Big Air at the base of Whistler Mountain. Added the Moving Pictures film festival, the Backbone Enduro Vertical Challenge and the all-night 'Heaven' event in the Conference Centre ballroom. Record April skier numbers on both mountains.
venue_name: Whistler Village, Whistler Mountain and Blackcomb Mountain

name: 2015 World Ski & Snowboard Festival
description: Programme included the Bud Light Freeride Club Series, the 72-Hour Filmmaker Showdown, the outdoor concert series and the photography competition. The Showcase Showdown pro men's winner earned a start in the festival's Monster Energy Shred Show.

name: 2018 World Ski & Snowboard Festival
description: First edition after Vail Resorts' acquisition, shortened to six days. The Saudan Couloir Ski Race Extreme returned after a 20-year break.

name: 2019 World Ski & Snowboard Festival
description: Shortened again to five days.

name: 2020 World Ski & Snowboard Festival
catalog_status_note: Cancelled due to COVID-19.

name: 2021 World Ski & Snowboard Festival
catalog_status_note: Cancelled due to COVID-19.

name: 2022 World Ski & Snowboard Festival
description: Returned after two cancelled years in a scaled-down weekend format under Gibbons Whistler ownership. Exact dates not sourced.

name: 2025 World Ski & Snowboard Festival
description: Whistler Blackcomb's own 60th anniversary timeline calls 2025 the festival's 30th anniversary; wssf.com calls 2026 the 30-year anniversary. Dates not sourced.

name: 2026 World Ski & Snowboard Festival
description: Billed by the organisers as the 30-year anniversary. Snow programme included The Pipe (invited-rider mini pipe session), The Grind ski and snowboard rail jam series, Safety Shred Days, the Powder Puck Classic and the Slush Cup at Glacier Creek; plus Intersection and the 72-Hour Filmmaker Showdown.

name: 2001 World Snowboarding Championships
description: Slopestyle, jib jam and superpipe. Pique's year-in-review reported that American riders took most of the wins. Sponsored by WestBeach Sports, which cancelled its own WestBeach Classic to fund it.

name: 2012 World Snowboarding Championships
description: Organised by Snowboard-VM 2012 AS, owned by The Arctic Challenge, the Norwegian Snowboard Federation and Oslo Vinterpark. Described as the first world championships run by snowboarders since 1999. The Arctic Challenge did not run under its own name in 2012 as far as the sources I opened show.

name: The World Championships of Snowboarding 2016
description: 400 athlete spots across the three disciplines, allocated through national snowboard association quotas. Billed as the pinnacle event of the 2016 tour, and the meeting at which the TTR tour champions were crowned.

name: 1983 World Snowboarding Championships
description: The first snowboard halfpipe contest. Organised by Tom Sims with Mike Chantry; the pipe was pushed up with a snowcat and then dug out by hand. Riders on Jake Burton's East Coast team objected to counting halfpipe in the overall standings and reportedly threatened a boycott. No exact date found in any source opened; Sims' USPTO service-mark registration claims first use in commerce on 15 February 1983, which is the closest thing to a contemporaneous date. CONFLICT: a 2014 Snowboard Magazine piece on the Sims Retro World Championships refers to 'the 1982 2nd World Snowboard Championships in Soda Springs', implying a 1981 or 1982 first edition; every other source opened calls 1983 the inaugural year.

name: 1984 World Snowboarding Championships
description: Tahoe Quarterly states Terry Kidwell won the halfpipe at Soda Springs in 1984 and 1985; the Sierra Sun halfpipe history says Kidwell 'won the following two years' after Eddie Hargraves' 1983 win. No date, no full podium and no other disciplines confirmed.

name: 1985 World Snowboarding Championships
description: Second of Terry Kidwell's two Soda Springs halfpipe wins per Tahoe Quarterly. Note that Breckenridge's own history page claims Breckenridge 'hosts the first snowboard World Cup' in 1985 - a different event from this championship, and itself disputed (see open questions).

name: 1986 World Snowboarding Championships
description: First Breckenridge edition, March 1986, on a hand-dug halfpipe on Peak 9. Breckenridge had lifted its snowboarding ban in 1984, the first major Colorado resort to do so. Paul Alden persuaded Breckenridge management to accept the halfpipe as a legitimate competitive format; Swatch was a major sponsor and the event drew national media. Greg Stump filmed it for 'Maltese Flamingo' (1986). Terry Kidwell is reported to have won the halfpipe again in 1986 after the championships moved to Colorado (Tahoe Quarterly) - treated here as unconfirmed, no result row written. No full podium found in any source opened. Sources give only the month, not the days.

name: 1987 World Snowboarding Championships
description: DATE CONFLICT. The Snowboarder/TransWorld 1980s timeline and Paul Alden's obituaries put the second Breckenridge Worlds in March 1987 - specifically, NASBA was formed on 8 March 1987, 'the day after' the championships ended, which implies the event finished 7 March 1987. TransWorld's halfpipe history instead dates the 1987 Breckenridge World Championships to 2-5 April 1987 and calls its pipe (about 200 feet long with near-vertical six-foot walls) the best in snowboarding to that point. Dates left null. Jose Fernandes is reported to have won the giant slalom on an asymmetrical board (snowboarding8090.com) - not corroborated, no result row written. Craig Kelly's published timeline lists 'Swatch World Championships' results for 1987 and 1988, which is the strongest indication that the Breckenridge Worlds carried Swatch's name.

name: WSF South America Tour 2012
description: Seven stops: Urban Rail Jam, Parque Arauco, Santiago, Chile (7 Jul); Roxy Snow Jam, Valle Nevado (8 Aug); Columbia Slopestyle, Valle Nevado (11 Aug); Mall Sport South America Rookie Fest, Valle Nevado (26 Aug); Rip Curl The Gump Big Air Show, Valle Nevado (August, exact date not given); Rey del Park, El Colorado (2 Sep); and a 2-Star indoor slopestyle grand finale in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (24-26 Oct). Counted for TTR and WSF ranking lists.

name: X Games Oslo 2016
description: First X Games to stage summer and winter disciplines in the same city; skateboard street ran at the Skur 13 warehouse at Filipstad Harbour. Announcement coverage places snowboard superpipe at Oslo Winter Park on 26 February and snowboard/ski big air at Toyen on 27 February. First X Games to include women's ski and snowboard big air.
venue_name: Oslo Winter Park (snowboard superpipe) and Toyen (big air)

name: X Games Norway 2017 (Hafjell)
description: Men's and women's snowboard slopestyle and big air. Hafjell Resort reports 17,500 spectators and Norwegian athletes taking 3 gold, 2 silver and 1 bronze of 8 golds. No superpipe.

name: X Games Norway 2018 (Oslo)
description: Indoor/urban big air edition held in May. Dates are taken from the title of an ESPN Press Room release ('SAVE THE DATE: X Games Norway 2018 May 16-20 in Oslo'); espnpressroom.com returned HTTP 403 to this researcher so the body of the release was not read. Venue attribution to Telenor Arena is inferred from the 2019 edition and is NOT confirmed - treat as unverified.

name: X Games Norway 2019 (Oslo)
description: Indoor edition combining winter and summer disciplines under one roof: men's and women's snowboard and ski big air, skateboard street, and Moto X. Only 31 August 2019 was confirmed as a competition date; the event ran over more than one day and the full date range was not established.

name: X Games Norway 2020 (Hafjell)
description: Big air on the Saturday, slopestyle on the Sunday, including a Knuckle Huck (recorded as 'other'). Final X Games Norway edition. Mark McMorris took his 19th career X Games medal with gold in snowboard big air here, passing Shaun White's winter medal record.

name: X-Trail Jam, January 2001
description: Launch edition. Wikipedia's results table lists two 2001 events, January and December, so the contest ran twice in the calendar year as it shifted to a December slot.

name: X-Trail Jam, December 2001
description: Second event of the 2001 calendar year; belongs to the 2001/02 season.

name: X-Trail Jam 2004
description: Fifth running. Quarterpipe used a jam-session format; straight jump ran best-of-two runs in qualifying and switched to a jam session for the final. Japanese coverage describes the event as the signal that winter has started.

name: Nissan X-Trail Jam 2008
description: Last year in the Wikipedia results table. Later editions are referenced by Method Mag and WSF but were not confirmed year by year in this pass.

name: NISSAN X-TRAIL e-4ORCE RAIL JAM 2023
description: Revival of the X-Trail name after 14 years, moved from the indoor Tokyo Dome format to an outdoor street/rail course at a ski resort.

name: Zillertal Vaelley Raelley 2025/26 (13th season)
description: 13th season, four stops: Hochzillertal-Kaltenbach (20-21 Dec 2025); Action-Park Kreuzwiese, Zillertal Arena (24-25 Jan 2026); PenkenPark Mayrhofen (28 Feb - 1 Mar 2026); Betterpark Hintertux, Hintertux Glacier (25-26 Apr 2026). Results count for the World Snowboard Points List and the World Rookie Ranking. The 2024/25 season was the 12th and also had four events.
